Text.Text: Primal Overrun. You already put it through the den and out the other side. Nothing left in these thickets tests you the way that did. Go run with your beast; that is the whole lesson now.

Stop. Right there. One more careless step and the ground under you remembers you different than it does now. You have not bonded deep enough with a beast to walk this den yet. Come back when the two of you move like one animal, not two.

So you did not flinch. Good, flinching gets you killed twice as fast in there. My clan lost the Grotto Apex Den three generations back to off-world handlers who broke every beast they touched instead of binding it. The handlers are bones now, but the shell-backs they bred still hold the den, bred to charge anything that moves. Go into the den on Dathomir, put down six of the Young Shell-Backs, the ones holding the chambers nearest the way in, and bring me the Primal Overrun Grotto Track Slate from their nest. Any Young Shell-Back will do, every shell-back in that den answers to the same handlers' lessons. But a kill only teaches you something after your own beast has hit the target. Any beast you own can do this, whatever its role or level. A normal attack is enough; the killing blow can come from you or your party. Kills that never felt your beast's weight prove nothing. It still reads clan trails.

Take this key. Go through the Hidden Cave north-east of this landing, on through the jungle into the Desert, west across it to the Tribe Village, then north-west into the Grottos. Follow the canyon north-east to the entrance on the Grottos' east side; it lets you into the south end of the Grotto Caverns. The den is a short walk north-west of there, on the west side by the water: a moss-topped rock mound with a dark cave mouth. That mouth is the way in. Get in, get the slate, get out.

The den was ours before the handlers came in from off-world with their goad-sticks and their contracts. They did not want the beasts tamed, just broken and pointed. We fought them for it and lost good hunters to beasts that had stopped being beasts. The handlers lost worse in the end; what they broke turned on them. I do not go back in for pride. I go when the den asks for a debt paid, and right now it is asking through you.

Every clan hunter that ever ran that den marked a slate like it: where the good trails run, where the ground lies to you. The handlers used it to route their beasts onto killing floors, and it still lies in the nest they left behind. Bring it back whole and it goes back to reading trails instead of routing slaughter.

Shell-backs, the young ones. Armored, heavy, bred to charge anything that moves and never ask why. They come in a line and they do not turn easy, so do not stand where they are headed. Watch the ground, not just the charge.
The den has not finished with you. Six Young Shell-Backs, struck by your own beast before they fall, and my slate out of their nest.
You made it out and you are not missing pieces. That is already better than the last two off-worlders who tried. Let's see the slate.
That is clan work, done right. The trails still remember how to read true because of it. Rest up. There is more of this if you want it, and I think you do.

Slate came back clean. That is one debt closer to paid. The Goad-Scarred Shell-Backs, the older ones deeper in, are worse; the handlers drove them so long they charge before anything gives the word. Put down five of them in the Grotto Apex Den, again after a hit from your own beast; any Goad-Scarred Shell-Back counts. Then bring me the Primal Overrun Resonant Fang Charm. One of them still wears it on the collar the handlers bolted on.
Same gate in the Grotto Caverns, deeper trail this time. The key still opens for you; the den does not forget a hand it has already let through. Go quiet, come back with the charm.

The young ones still hesitate before a charge. The older ones had the hesitation beaten out of them. The handlers turned Primal Overrun into something done to an animal, not with one. A charge that is not chosen is not a charge, it is a shove. I want that shove gone from the den before it breeds into the next ones.

The resonant fang charm hums when a beast is about to break its bond and run wild: an old clan trick, to know fear from fury before it is too late. The handlers hung it on their beasts so they would know when to push harder. Cruelty with a warning bell they ignored on purpose.

Because the last time I went into that den my own beast did not come out, and I put down what came out instead of him. I can send you. I cannot send myself back through that gate yet. Maybe not ever. That is mine to carry, not yours to fix.
Five of the old shell-backs still charging around in there like they own the ground. Bring me that fang charm when they do not.
You have got their hum on you; I can feel it from here. Hand it over before it starts working on you too.
Good. The warning bell is back where it belongs. You are starting to move like someone the den might actually let leave twice.

You have done more in that den than most clan-born manage. Past the shell-backs is Handler's Rancor, a bull rancor the handlers raised from a calf and taught to shove instead of bond. He has killed alone before, and he will kill you alone too. Do not go at him by yourself; bring two you would trust to carry your beast out if you cannot. Put him down and bring me the Primal Overrun Cracked Apex Totem that hangs from his harness.
Same gate. The ground past it is not the same; Handler's Rancor does not wait for you to be ready, so do not wait either. Go in together, come out together.

He came from clan stock. The calf of the last rancor my clan ever bonded, taken with the den. The handlers chained him and taught him the shove worked better than the bond. The shell-backs learned the shove from him, and he learned it from his sire. Cut that off at the root.

The cracked apex totem used to mark a den's true alpha trail, back when the den had one worth marking. The handlers cracked it and hung it on him to say the trail was theirs now. Bring it back whole enough to read and I will know the trail again.

Because he does not tire and he does not miss, and a beast that has been shoved instead of bonded does not know how to quit either. One hunter alone against that and the den gets a new pair of bones to remember. Two more blades beside yours, and he has to split his rage between three throats instead of one. That is not cowardice. That is how the den has always hunted anything worth calling an alpha.
Handler's Rancor is still down there teaching the wrong lesson. Go finish him, with company, like I said.
You are standing. All three of you, I hope, wherever the rest of your hunt is now. Let's see what he was carrying.
The apex totem, whole and readable. That is the first true blow against what this den became. Rest. The oldest shell-backs in the deep den will have felt this.

Four are left that matter: the Den Elder Shell-Backs, the oldest in the den, the first of their kind the handlers ever broke. Every charge the young ones throw, these four threw first. They hold the deep floor together, not alone, so you do not go alone either. Put all four down in the deepest part of the den, after your own beast has struck each one, and bring me the Primal Overrun Den-Mother's Fang Token from the deep nest they guard. Any Den Elder Shell-Back counts.
Same gate. They will have felt Handler's Rancor fall by now, so expect them ready. Go in together, stay together; that is not a suggestion with four of them.

They are the first shell-backs the handlers ever broke, and the biggest. They hold the deep floor shoulder to shoulder, shells locked, and when they move it is all at once. The young ones learned to charge from watching them. Patient, heavy, and wrong.

Every den worth the name has a den-mother somewhere in its bones, the first beast the clan ever bonded true, not broken. Her fang token passed hunter to hunter as proof you knew the difference. The handlers buried it in the deep nest so no hunter could ever claim it again. Whole in your hand, it is proof the difference still means something.

Nothing like what they teach. A proper overrun is your beast choosing the same target you already chose, same breath, same moment, not a beast driven at something because a stick told it to. You will know it when it happens with yours. It feels like agreement, not a shove.
Four of them still holding that deep nest like it is theirs. Go break them, together, and bring the token back whole.
Company is still breathing, and so are you. That token had better be in one piece. Hand it here.
Whole, and warm, like it has been waiting. One beast left down there, and it is the one that made all the others. The trail is short now, so I will say it plain: you have earned this last one.

Last one. Old Rancor is the old bull, the sire of Handler's Rancor, the last rancor my clan ever bonded. The handlers spent years teaching him to charge on their word, and when they were gone he kept charging on his own. Every shove in that den started with him. Bring your two back; his overrun does not slow down for numbers, and one hunter alone just becomes one more body the den has to explain. The den keeps no token for this. His fall is the proof, all of it.
Then go. Gate is open same as always. This is the one I cannot tell you how to win, only that you will not, alone.

The others learned the overrun from him in pieces. He never lost the whole of it. He charges with everything he is, all at once, no hesitation: the true version you have been chasing with your own beast, only aimed at cruelty instead of company. That is what makes him dangerous. That is also what you are about to take from him.

Because his charge is everything at once, and it goes through anything standing alone in front of it. Three of you from three angles, and he has to choose, and choosing is the one thing that charge was never built to do twice in a breath. Alone, you are just the next thing he does not have to choose between.

It goes back to being a den instead of a lesson in cruelty. Whether my clan ever walks back in, I do not know yet. That part is mine to decide, after. Yours is just to make sure there is a den left worth deciding about.
He is still down there, still charging the old lessons into the den. Go end it. Together.
Quiet. The whole den has gone quiet, and it has never once done that in my lifetime. Tell me it is him.

Then it is done, and it is yours: the overrun the way it is supposed to run, beast and hunter, one push, one choice. My clan lost this den three generations back. You just gave me a reason to think about walking through that gate again myself. Go run with your beast. You have earned the ground under both of you.
Back to it.
I'll clear the six and bring your slate.
What happened to your clan's den?
What's this track slate to you?
What am I walking into down there?
Not today. I need to think.
Here's the Primal Overrun Grotto Track Slate.
Back to it.
I'll put down the five and bring the charm.
What makes the old ones worse than the young?
What's the fang charm for?
Why can't you go in yourself?
Give me time first.
Here's the Primal Overrun Resonant Fang Charm.
Back to it.
I'll bring company and take Handler's Rancor down.
Who is Handler's Rancor to you?
What's the apex totem?
Why can't I face him alone?
Not until I've got my two.
Here's the Primal Overrun Cracked Apex Totem, whole.
Back to it.
I'll take my company back in for the four.
Who are the Den Elder Shell-Backs?
What's the den-mother's fang token?
What does a proper overrun feel like?
My company needs rest first.
Here's the Primal Overrun Den-Mother's Fang Token, whole.
Back to it.
We're going in for Old Rancor.
What makes him different from Handler's Rancor and the Den Elders?
Why does his overrun need three of us and not one?
What happens to the den, after?
Not until my company's ready.
It's done. He's down.
